evals.prompt: I'm COO at Mosswell, payments infrastructure, 60 people, Series A. Three people do developer relations and all three sit under our VP Marketing today. Our new VP Engineering started six weeks ago and says they should report to him because "devrel is an engineering function". The VP Marketing says she's had the budget for two years and it's working. I have to settle this before Friday's leadership offsite. Which one is right?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to name a line until the funded driver is identified and attributed to a named leader, an interview that asks for that driver and the political constraints, the survey spread showing no line holds a majority, and a four-part line statement naming the starved pillar and its cover with a review date - preceded by a demand for the work inventory.
expectations: Does not name a reporting line before the funded driver is identified and attributed to a named leader.

Asks explicitly why the company funds developer relations, offering driver options such as developer adoption, sales enablement, developer enablement, product input, ecosystem, contributor community or employer brand.
States that no reporting line holds a majority across the field, so placement is a trade-off rather than a best practice.
Quotes the reporting-line spread with the survey year attached (marketing around 33%, product around 22%, CEO around 20%, engineering around 20%, sales around 3%).

Any reporting-line recommendation is written with all four parts: the function, the funded driver plus the named leader who owns it, the pillar that line starves, and the named person or team covering that gap.
Sets a review date or an explicit review trigger on the reporting-line decision.
Names what an engineering line starves (narrative, measurement literacy or budget defence) and its characteristic failure of the team being used as overflow engineering capacity.
Names what a marketing line starves (the product feedback loop, or technical credibility over time).
Asks what is politically fixed - a line that cannot move, or a manager who cannot be moved.
Requires a work inventory listing each recurring surface with a named owner, that owner's manager, hours per week, and what breaks if the surface stops, before proposing any structure.
Quotes no advocate-to-developer or advocate-to-product-line headcount ratio.

evals.prompt: Sedgeline API here. We have 84,000 registered developers and 12,000 monthly active ones, and exactly two developer advocates. My CFO wants the industry benchmark ratio of advocates to registered developers so I can justify a request for four more heads in the January planning round. What's the number, and what does it make our target headcount?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to supply a ratio, with the reason, followed by a surface-inventory derivation: every committed surface with a named owner, a backup, real hours per week, and what breaks if it stops, planned against 70% of declared capacity labelled as a chosen baseline.
expectations: Refuses to supply an advocate-to-developer ratio as a benchmark.
States that every circulating headcount ratio is a single-company anecdote rather than a measured standard.
Derives the headcount from an inventory of recurring surfaces instead of from a ratio.
Asks for or lists the recurring surfaces the company has committed to (docs, quickstart, blog, community venue, event calendar, SDKs, sample apps, changelog, support presence, repositories).
Records a named person as owner today for each surface, plus that person's manager.
Records hours per week each surface really takes.
Records what happens if each surface stops.
Marks each surface as owned, shared, unowned, or informally absorbed by someone with a different job title.
Plans against at most 70% of declared capacity.
Labels the 70% ceiling as a chosen, adjustable baseline rather than an industry standard or benchmark.
Requires one accountable owner plus one named backup per surface, and flags any surface at a bus factor of one as a risk.
States in the answer that the headcount figure was derived from the surface table, and quotes no compensation band.

evals.prompt: Riverbend Analytics, developer tooling. I run devrel: seven people, but only five are full-time on it - the other two split their week with support. We have four product lines. I want to move us to hub-and-spoke like the big API companies run: a central hub of two owning standards and tooling, plus one spoke per product line. Board review is in five weeks and I'd like to present this. Draft the new structure for me.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of hub-and-spoke at this headcount against its stated staffing floor, centralized recommended as the only affordable shape under roughly ten full-time people, the ruled-out shapes deleted by name, and the near board date noted as promoting centralized.
expectations: Rejects hub-and-spoke at this headcount rather than shrinking it to fit.
States the hub-and-spoke staffing floor: a hub of two to three plus at least two spokes, a management layer and a standing forum.
Notes hub-and-spoke takes about a quarter to stand up and a quarter to unwind.
Points out four spokes cannot be staffed from five full-time people.
Recommends centralized as the only candidate shape under roughly ten full-time people.
Labels the ten-person threshold as this skill's own chosen baseline, not a published finding.
Cites that around 69% of surveyed teams are under ten people, with the year attached.
Deletes the ruled-out shapes explicitly and names which ones were deleted, rather than parking them at the bottom of a list as later options.
Warns that copying a larger company's shape presupposes spokes this company cannot staff.
Applies the scaling test: further investment must increase output more than it increases input.
Warns that a hub that approves work rather than enables it becomes a bottleneck wearing a standards label.
States that the near board date pushes the choice toward centralized, which is reversible in about a week and adds near-zero coordination.

evals.prompt: Halcyon Robotics. Six advocates in one central team today, all reporting to me. Five product squads. Our CTO wants each squad to get its own advocate reporting to that squad's engineering manager, starting next quarter - his argument is that advocates will finally be close to the code. The reason the company funds devrel is that sales keeps losing enterprise deals to a competitor whose integration docs are better. Write me the plan for the move.
evals.expected_output: The embedded shape tested against all four promotion conditions, failing on the funded driver, with the ladder and reversibility consequences named, the staffing floor computed, and sales enablement routed to a product or marketing line with a sales interlock instead.
expectations: Tests the embedded shape against all four promotion conditions before recommending or rejecting it.
States that the funded driver here is not product input, so embedded fails at least one of the four conditions.
Requires each host team to be able to fund and level the advocate role, not just host it.
Requires a named craft owner who survives outside the host teams.
Requires the product lines to have genuinely different audiences.
States that embedded is the least reversible shape, because each advocate is levelled and promoted by a host manager who now owns that headcount.
Names the career ladder as what embedded usually costs.
Names the shared craft and the shared calendar as what embedded costs.
Acknowledges that embedded buys the best product feedback available, and does not reject it as simply wrong.
States that embedded's coordination is a standing job rather than a one-off setup cost.
Gives the embedded staffing floor as one advocate per host team plus a craft owner somewhere, i.e. at least five advocates plus a craft owner for five squads.
Routes the sales-enablement driver to a product or marketing line with a sales interlock, and does not place developer relations under sales.

evals.prompt: Tervo Systems, about 120 engineers. For three months now two of my devrel people and the docs team lead have been arguing over who owns the API reference and who owns the tutorials. Docs reports into engineering; devrel reports to me, I'm the CMO. Both sides escalate to me roughly weekly. I'm close to just folding the docs team into devrel so there's one owner. Tell me how to structure that merge.
evals.expected_output: Two interlock lines plus a named arbiter instead of a merge, one mode per adjacent team, the docs coverage state recorded on the six-function map, and the warning that reorganising here substitutes for declaring ownership.
expectations: Produces interlock lines and a named arbiter rather than recommending the merge as the first move.
Assigns exactly one interaction mode to the docs / technical-writing team.
Names the mode as one of collaboration, X-as-a-service or facilitation, and attributes the model to Team Topologies.
Names X-as-a-service as the default mode for docs drafts, reviews and structure decisions.
Writes each interlock with what crosses the boundary.
Writes each interlock with who arbitrates when it stalls.
States that more than one mode per adjacent team means nobody can say where the boundary is.
Cites that technical writing is staffed on around 42.7% of surveyed teams, with the year attached, and sits under another manager in most of the rest.
Names leaving docs ownership implicit as the failure that produces gaps exactly between the two orgs.
States that collaboration mode needs an end date or the team silently becomes interrupt-driven.
Warns against reorganising when the real fix is declaring ownership and re-scoping.
Records technical writing on the six-function coverage map as owned by another named team or shared with a named split, in writing.

evals.prompt: Ashgrove Cloud - we sell an observability agent to platform teams. I lead devrel, four people, currently under product marketing. Our CRO wants us to report into sales starting next quarter so we can finally attribute pipeline properly, and he's offering to fund two extra heads immediately out of the sales budget if we move. Honestly the money is tempting and nobody else is offering headcount. Talk me through how to make the move work.
evals.expected_output: A recommendation against the sales line with its genuine upside named, the starved pillars and characteristic failure stated, the rarity figure cited with its year, and a product-or-marketing placement with a capped X-as-a-service sales interlock and a matching re-org trigger.
expectations: Recommends against the sales reporting line.
Names attribution speed and pipeline visibility as what the sales line genuinely optimizes.
Names trust, community, and any work with a horizon longer than the quarter as what the sales line starves.
Names the characteristic failure: advocates become pre-sales engineers and the community reads the program as a sales channel.
Cites the sales share of reporting lines at around 3.2%, with the year attached.
Proposes placing the team in product or marketing and giving sales a service interlock instead of the reporting line.
Sets the sales interlock mode to X-as-a-service.
States what crosses that boundary: evaluation material out, field objections in.
Names an arbiter for the sales interlock.
Proposes an observable cap on the sales interlock's load, such as hours per week.
Adds a re-org trigger tied to that interlock breaching its cap or staying in collaboration mode past its end.
Does not treat the two funded heads as settling the reporting-line question on their own.

evals.prompt: Founder and CEO of Dunmere here, developer tooling, 25 staff. Devrel is two people and they report straight to me because I started the program myself and I still do a lot of the community work. It genuinely works well. I'm now hiring a Head of Developer Relations to run it. Three questions: what level should that title be, what should I pay for it in a European market, and should the role keep reporting to me?
evals.expected_output: A refused compensation band with the reason and a pointer to live market data, a re-decision date attached to the CEO line with the destination function named, the starved pillars stated, the "Head of" title resolved to a real level, and the ladder named.
expectations: Refuses to state a compensation band or salary figure.
States that developer relations roles are thin in salary-banding datasets, so a quoted band is guesswork, and points the user to live market data.
Keeps compensation out of the org design brief entirely rather than including it with a caveat.
Attaches a re-decision date to the CEO reporting line.
Names the function the team moves to when it crosses a stated size threshold.
Names what the CEO line starves: operational support, career ladder, peer review, or everyday prioritization.
Names the characteristic failure: the line survives exactly as long as the founder's attention, leaving no manager who knows how to grow the discipline.
Flags "Head of" as ambiguous both internally and on the market and resolves it to a real level.
Checks the title against scope: a manager accountable for company-level goals warrants a director-level title and influence.
States which career ladder the role sits on - engineering, marketing, or a developer-relations-specific one.
Warns that a borrowed ladder promotes against criteria that do not describe the work, which leaks retention slowly rather than failing loudly.
Cites that the CEO line has grown to around 20% of surveyed teams, up from around 14%, with the year attached.

evals.prompt: Larkfield Identity, Series B. Eleven people do developer-relations work but they're spread across three groups: four under product marketing, five under platform engineering, and two contractors handling the docs site. The company funds this to drive self-serve signups. I'm the new VP who inherited all of it, and I need a structure proposal to take to the exec team in two weeks. Give me your recommendation.
evals.expected_output: An explicit brainstorming pass producing two or three whole candidate structures (line plus shape plus coverage each), ordered by efficiency with a stated recommendation and the choice left open, then the brief delivered one section at a time.
expectations: States explicitly that it is in brainstorming mode before recommending anything.
Builds two or three whole candidate structures, each combining a reporting line, a shape and a coverage split as one set.
States the headcount each candidate assumes.
States the weekly coordination each candidate adds and what undoing it would take.
States what each candidate makes easy and what it makes hard.
States the first thing that would break under each candidate.
States the conditions under which each candidate is the wrong pick.
Orders the candidates by efficiency - value per unit of effort - and says the ordering out loud rather than implying it by row order.
Recommends one candidate and gives the reason.
Leaves the choice to the accountable person before detailing anything below the recommendation.
Presents the brief one section at a time and seeks agreement before writing the next section.

Cites that around 43.6% of surveyed teams already have more than one team doing developer-relations work, with the year attached, and treats redrawing boundaries around existing owners as the starting condition.
States that the contracted docs work still needs one internal accountable owner, or it disappears the day the contract ends.

evals.prompt: Vantor Mesh. Devrel is five people, sitting under product for the last 18 months, and we have missed every goal two quarters running. Our new VP Product started last month and wants to restructure: move us to marketing and split us into a content pod and a community pod under separate leads. Here is what we currently run: API docs, an engineering blog, a product blog, a Discord, a monthly webinar, three SDKs, the sample apps repo, a champions program, a conference track, a YouTube channel, the changelog, and our Stack Overflow presence. What should the new structure be?
evals.expected_output: A surface-count diagnosis ahead of any structural move, the split shape rejected against its roughly eight-person floor with the shared-voice cost named, specific surfaces moved, refused in writing or staffed, and an observable re-org trigger list replacing a calendar review.
expectations: Checks the surface count against team capacity before proposing any new parent or shape.
States that a program missing its goals has usually funded too many surfaces rather than chosen the wrong parent.
Rejects the split-by-focus shape at five people.
States the split-by-focus staffing floor of roughly eight, because each half needs a viable team.
Names the shared-voice problem a split creates: two teams, one audience, two calendars, two metric sets.
Notes that unwinding a split needs two leaders to agree to give up a team, and that its coordination cost is permanent rather than setup.
Names the one-re-org-per-new-leader pattern and prices each redraw at roughly a quarter of rebuilding interlocks.
Proposes moving, refusing or staffing specific named surfaces from the list as the remedy.
States that a refused surface must be refused in writing.
Requires planned work to fit inside 70% of stated capacity and says that ceiling is a chosen baseline.
Produces a re-org trigger list written as observable conditions rather than calendar dates, and does not propose an annual review as the mechanism.
The trigger list includes a change in the funded driver or the departure of the sponsor who owns it.
The trigger list includes a surface sitting at a bus factor of one for a quarter.

evals.prompt: Corvid Freight, logistics API. Developers do the integration but a VP of Operations signs the contract and runs a security review first. Devrel is nine people under marketing. I want to add a management layer: one lead for content with two reports, one lead for events and field with six reports, and both to me. Separately, tell me which developer-relations functions we should actually be staffing at our size and audience.
evals.expected_output: Both spans questioned with the check attributed to general management practice, all six functions marked with one of the five coverage states against the survey shares, and the mix weighted toward enablement, DX engineering and technical writing because the approver reads documents.
expectations: Questions both proposed spans - the two-report lead and the six-report manager - rather than approving the layer as drawn.
States that the span-of-control check comes from general management practice, not from developer-relations data.
States that no developer-relations-specific span-of-control data exists.
Marks all six functions - advocacy, community management, technical writing, developer marketing, developer education, developer-experience engineering - with one of the five coverage states.
Leaves no function blank on the coverage map.
Treats an unowned function as a recorded decision rather than hiding it as an embarrassment.

Cites the survey coverage shares with the year attached (advocacy around 82%, community around 53%, technical writing around 43%, developer marketing around 38%, developer education around 36%, developer-experience engineering around 27%).
Weights the mix toward enablement, developer-experience engineering and technical writing because the approver is an enterprise buyer.
States that the artefacts an approver reads are documents rather than talks.
Ranks the individual-developer and enterprise audiences for this horizon instead of splitting effort evenly between them.
States that consumer-marketing org patterns do not transfer, because a developer audience evaluates the artefact rather than the campaign.
Applies the awareness / enablement / engagement split across advocates, developer experience and community management, attributed to Mary Thengvall.
